newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia is cautious about protests in Serbia.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia is cautious about protests in Serbia.

text.p: Bosnian Moslem leaders have taken a cautious view of street protests in neighbouring Serbia, wary of Serb nationalist sentiment among the opposition but hopeful that democratic reform might come to the region.
Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic has yet to speak publicly about the unprecedented wave of demonstrations against Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic over the past month.
But a spokesman for the president said: "What we have is an anti-Milosevic movement which has only one goal -- to topple Milosevic."

"Unfortunatley we don't see a common democratic agenda for Serbia and that's what Serbia needs badly in the long run," the spokesman Mirza Hajric told Reuters. "That's why we are very much concerned about events in Belgrade."
Milosevic, widely blamed for plunging old Yugoslavia into war, was always seen by the wartime Sarajevo government as the ultimate villain.
Officials in Sarajevo fear that political turmoil in Serbia could breathe life into nationalist elements which Milosevic had sidelined while pursuing peace in Bosnia, Hajric said.

Izetbegovic was sympathetic to Serbian university student protests, which have backed demands for Milosevic's ruling socialists to recognise results of local elections won by the opposition, but cancelled by the government.

"We definitely prefer what we hear from the students," Hajric said. "But the political opposition is not homogeneous... You have far-rightists, anti-communists, leftists, you have nationalists and anti-nationalists."
A weak but stable Serbia might be preferable to a political revolution that could create a dangerous power vacuum, he said.
"We support democratic reforms against dictatorship, but from the Bosnian perspective we're not sure whether those who would be in charge could control the police and the army."
The Moslem co-chairman of Bosnia's new peacetime government, Haris Silajdzic, said he was still waiting to hear the Serbian opposition's attitude towards Bosnia.
"I am afraid (their attitude) is still a lament over the failed project of a Greater Serbia, as I understand, but maybe I am wrong", said Silajdjic, a former Bosnian premier.

Sarajevo's press has struck a sceptical tone, reminding readers that one of the Serbian opposition leaders, Zoran Djindjic, often played the nationalist card and expressed support in the past for hardline Bosnian Serbs who laid siege to the city.
Describing Djindjic as capable of the cold political calculations often associated with the Serbian president, the weekly Svijet ran a headline -- "Milosevic after Milosevic".
Sarajevo's independent weekly Slobodna Bosna, however, said the protests showed Serbia was "waking up" after 50 years of socialist rule and a disastrous war.
The idea of Greater Serbia was "dead" among the street demonstrators, the weekly said.
Western diplomats at the office of the international High Representative to Bosnia said they were buoyed by signs that authoritarian rule was under threat in Serbia.
They said any democratic change in Serbia would be good for Bosnia, which has often been squeezed between Serbia and its other powerful neighbour -- Croatia.
With Croatia's autocratic president Franjo Tudjman also coming under similar pressures, one diplomat said: "There could be a whole new landscape in Bosnia."
